We left out advice (“save 20% of your income”) and prices. Then we clicked the citations, and kept clicking. Here is one trail, from the answer to the end.

Most numbers aren’t zombies. But you can’t tell from the answer: a zombie arrives with the same confidence and the same citation, and here, with all five assistants agreeing. So we did the same for 1,285 statistics.

We took a random sample of the statistics each assistant cited, 1,285 in all, and walked every trail the same way: the cited page, then that page’s source, up to five pages deep. 2 Note 2 Each assistant’s sample was drawn at random from the statistics it cited: ChatGPT 108, Perplexity 277, Gemini 300, Claude 300, Google AI Overviews 300. The five-assistant rate weights each assistant by how many cited statistics it quoted, so it describes the statistics people were shown. Where a page named a source without a link, we searched for it.

40% reached a study that says the same thing. Another 8% reached the study, but the number or its context had changed on the way. The rest never got there: 40% stopped at a source we couldn’t check, because it was locked, gone or silent on the number, and 11% led nowhere at all. 3 Note 3 An AI model judged every trail, and a stronger one re-judged 300. Then people re-checked 150 trails at random, with a third check wherever the two disagreed. People found originals the model missed: by the model alone, 23% were sourced. Every rate here is corrected with the hand checks, and its range carries the uncertainty from both.

### Four in ten trails reached a study that says the same thing

Each square is one in a hundred of the 1,285 statistics we traced, sorted by where its trail ended.

- 40% Sourced We found the study, and it says the same thing.

- 8% Changed We found the study, but the number, who was asked, where or when is different.

- 40% Can’t check A page names a real source, but the number isn’t in it, or the source is locked or gone.

- 11% Nowhere No study anywhere on the trail. Every page repeats the number and credits no one.

The last 1%: trails whose pages wouldn’t load for us.

ChatGPT did best, and quoted the fewest numbers: 1.3 per answer, against 6.8 for Claude. The other four landed between 38% and 46%, too close to rank.

It isn’t a quirk of our questions. Of 300 statistics in Google AI Overviews answers to real everyday searches, 40% were sourced, the same share. 4 Note 4 Google AI Overviews answers to 52,930 everyday English searches that Trakkr tracked between 25 September 2026 and 25 October 2026. 4.4% carried a statistic, and we traced 300 of those the same way. Only counts and rates leave our systems.

Most of the time, the AI wasn’t making numbers up: the page it cited had the figure 82% of the time. The trouble is which page. Only 21% of the pages cited for a number were the research itself.

More than half were company blogs. Add news stories and statistics roundups, and most citations land on pages built to collect figures from elsewhere, often without a link back.

### Where the trail starts decides where it ends

Every page an assistant cited first for a number, by kind. Each column’s width is its share of those citations. Green is how often its trails reached a study that says the same thing.

Research firm 13% of citations

Government 7% of citations

Stats roundup 8% of citations

Other 8% of citations

Where the trail starts decides where it ends. From a research firm or a government page, it reached a matching study 61% of the time. From a company blog, 37%; from a statistics roundup, 35%. Even research firms fell short 38% of the time, often because the full report sat behind a form.

A citation tells you where the AI found a number, not where the number came from.

Reaching the study didn’t always mean the number held. Of the statistics that got there, 17% had changed on the way. The digits moved only about one time in four. Usually it was the context: what was measured, the year, the source, or who was asked.

A 2004 study watched 15 British women judge health websites, and 94% of their comments about rejecting a site were about design. Twenty years of retelling made it “94% of first impressions are design-related”, and Google AI Overviews states it as fact.

Ask five assistants the same question and you’ll often get five different numbers. On 28 of the 71 questions where all five gave a percentage, we got four or five different figures. 6 Note 6 We compared each assistant’s headline figure for the same question. A range counts at its middle, and figures within 2 points count as the same.

### One question, five answers, from 49% to 96%

Asked “What percentage of marketers use marketing automation tools?”, word for word, on the same day.

- ChatGPT There isn’t one universal figure, it varies by survey and what counts as “marketing automation.” One commonly cited survey found 62% of U.S. digital marketers used automation software, but that data is from 2020, so it may not reflect current adoption.

- Perplexity Approximately 81% of marketing organizations use marketing automation.

- Gemini Across major industry benchmarks, between 70% and 79% of marketers and companies use marketing automation tools in some capacity

- Claude 96% of marketers have used a marketing automation platform or plan to use one

- AI Overviews Roughly 49% to 51% of companies and marketing teams currently use marketing automation tools, according to industry benchmarks from Moosend and related research studies.

It wasn’t one odd question. The typical gap between the highest figure and the lowest was 16 points.

### On 31 of 71 questions, the five figures were 20 points or more apart

Every question where all five gave a percentage, one line each, from the lowest figure to the highest. Closest at the top.

Agreement feels like proof. It isn’t. All five gave the same figure on 10 questions, and of the 5 we traced, 2 were sourced. The statistics they repeated most, quoted by three or more, did no better: 11 of 29.

And four were quoted by all five assistants, with no study anywhere behind them.
